While he was speaking these words, a woman lifted up her voice from the crowd and told him, “Happy is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you!”
But he replied, “No — happy instead are the ones who hear the word of God and guard it!”
As the crowds were thronging together, he began to say, “This generation is a wicked generation. It looks for a sign, yet no sign will be granted it except the sign of Jonah.{h}
For as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.

The queen of the South{i} will rise at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and look, something greater than Solomon is here.

At the judgment the men of Nineveh will rise up together with this generation and pass sentence on it, for they turned in repentance at Jonah’s proclamation; and look, here is something greater than Jonah.
“No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar or under a basket,{j} but on the lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light.
Your eye is the lamp of the body. When your eye is sound,{k} your whole body too is full of light; but when it is bad, your body too is in darkness.
Watch out, therefore, that the light within you is not darkness.
If then your whole body is full of light, with no part of it dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp shines on you with its gleam.”
When he had spoken, a Pharisee invited him to have a meal at his house; so he went in and reclined at table.
The Pharisee was surprised to see that he did not first wash{l} before the meal.
But the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.
Fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside as well?
Rather, give as alms what is within, and look, everything is clean for you.
“But woe to you Pharisees! You tithe mint and rue and every garden herb, yet pass over justice and the love of God. These you ought to have practiced, without neglecting the others.
Woe to you Pharisees! You love the front seats in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.
Woe to you! You resemble tombs that are not marked, which people walk on unawares.”{m}
In response one of the lawyers said to him, “Teacher, by saying this you are insulting us as well.”
He replied, “And woe to you lawyers! You weigh people down with loads that are crushing to carry, while you yourselves will not lay one finger on the loads.
Woe to you! You construct monuments for the prophets, whom your ancestors put to death.
Thus you testify that you approve of what your ancestors did; they did the killing, and you do the building.
For this reason also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they will kill and persecute,’
so that from this generation may be required the blood of all the prophets, poured out since the world was founded,
from Abel’s blood to the blood of Zechariah,{n} who met his death between the altar and the house. Yes, I say to you, it will be required from this generation.
Woe to you lawyers! You have carried off the key of knowledge. You yourselves have not entered, and those who were entering you have blocked.”
As he went out from there, the scribes and Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things,
lying in wait to catch him in something he might say.

notes.text: Father: many manuscripts expand the prayer to resemble Matt 6:9–13, reading “Our Father in heaven” here, adding “may your will be done, on earth as in heaven” after “may your kingdom come,” and adding “but rescue us from the evil one” (or “from evil”) at the end of 11:4. The shorter form is that of the Westcott–Hort text, with P75, Vaticanus, and others.
Bread for the coming day: Greek *epiousios*, a rare word of uncertain meaning; possibly “daily,” “needed,” or “for tomorrow.”
Testing: or “temptation.”
Shameless persistence: Greek *anaideia*, “shamelessness.” It is uncertain whether the shamelessness is that of the asker or of the sleeper, who would be shamed by refusing.
If his son asks for: many manuscripts add “bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for,” as in Matt 7:9.
Beelzebul: a name of uncertain meaning, perhaps “lord of the dwelling” or “lord of dung”; compare Baal-zebub, “lord of flies,” in 2 Kgs 1:2.
The finger of God: compare Exod 8:19.
Jonah: Hebrew for “dove.” Many manuscripts add “the prophet.”
The queen of the South: the queen of Sheba (1 Kgs 10:1–10).
Basket: Greek *modios*, a container holding about 2 gallons (8.75 liters).
Sound: Greek *haplous*, “single,” “sincere,” or “generous”; “bad” may also mean “stingy.”
Wash: Greek *baptizō*, here a ritual washing before meals.
Contact with a grave made a person ritually unclean (Num 19:16).
Zechariah: probably the priest stoned in the temple court (2 Chr 24:20–22), the last murder recorded in the Hebrew Bible, whose final book is Chronicles. The name means “Yahweh remembers.”

verses.text: In the meantime, as the crowd assembled in tens of thousands, until they were treading on one another, he started by addressing his disciples: “Beware, above all, of the Pharisees’ leaven, which is hypocrisy.
Nothing is covered over that will not be uncovered, nor secret that will not become known.
Therefore whatever you have said in the dark will be heard in the daylight, and what you have whispered into an ear in inner rooms will be proclaimed from the housetops.
“To you, my friends, I say: have no fear of those who kill the body and after that can do nothing further.
But I will show you whom to fear: fear him who, once he has killed, holds the power to throw into Gehenna.{a} Yes, I tell you, fear that one.
Five sparrows are sold for two small coins,{b} are they not? And yet not one of them is forgotten in God’s sight.
Why, even the hairs of your head have all been counted. Have no fear; you are worth more than a great many sparrows.
“I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before people, the Son of Man too will acknowledge before God’s angels;
but whoever disowns me in front of people will be disowned in front of God’s angels.
Everyone who utters a word against the Son of Man will receive forgiveness; but for the one who has blasphemed the Holy Spirit there will be no forgiveness.
When they bring you before synagogues and rulers and authorities, do not worry about how to defend yourselves or what to say;
For in that hour the Holy Spirit will instruct you in the things you must say.”
Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to share the inheritance with me.”
But he told him, “Man, who set me up as judge or arbitrator over the two of you?”
And he said to them, “Look out, and guard yourselves against greed of every kind; for even when someone has abundance, his life does not consist in his possessions.”
Then he told them a parable: “The land of a certain rich man yielded a heavy crop.
He reasoned with himself, ‘What shall I do? I have no room to store my produce.’
Then he said, ‘Here is what I will do: I will pull my barns down and build bigger ones, and there I will gather in all my grain and my goods.
And I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have plenty of goods [laid up for many years; take it easy, eat, drink,] enjoy yourself.”’{c}
But God told him, ‘Senseless man! On this night they are demanding your soul back from you. And all you have prepared — who will own it then?’
[So it is with anyone who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.]”{d}
Then he told his disciples, “For this reason I say to you, stop fretting over your life — what to eat — or over your body — what to wear.
Life is more than food, and the body more than clothing.
Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have no storeroom or barn, and still God feeds them. Of how much greater value are you than the birds!
And which of you, by fretting, is able to add an hour{e} to the length of his life?
If then you cannot do even so small a thing, why be anxious about the rest?
Consider how the lilies grow: they neither toil nor spin. Yet I tell you, not even Solomon in all his splendor was robed like one of these.
If God clothes in this way the grass of the field, which is here today and is tossed into an oven tomorrow, how much more will he clothe you, you people of little faith!
So do not be searching for what to eat and what to drink, and do not hang in suspense.
For all the nations of the world chase after these things, and your Father knows you need them.
Instead, seek his kingdom,{f} and these things will be added to you.
“Do not be afraid, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom.
Sell your property and give alms. Make yourselves purses that do not wear out, an unfailing treasure in the heavens, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys.
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be as well.
“Keep your belts fastened{g} and your lamps lit,
Be like servants who are expecting their master on his way back from a marriage feast, ready to open for him the moment he arrives and knocks.
Blessed are those slaves whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly I tell you, he will tie on an apron, have them recline at table, and come and wait on them.
Whether he comes before midnight or after it,{h} and finds them so, blessed are they.
Be sure of this: had the householder known the hour the thief would come, he would not have allowed his house to be dug through.{i}
You also, be prepared, since at an hour you do not imagine, the Son of Man comes.”
Then Peter asked, “Lord, is it to us that you are speaking this parable, or to all people too?”
The Lord answered, “Who, then, is the trustworthy, prudent manager whom his lord will appoint over his servants to hand out their portion of grain at the right time?
Blessed is that slave whom his master on arrival finds doing so.
I tell you truthfully, he will appoint him over everything he possesses.
But if that slave says in his heart, ‘My master is taking his time in coming,’ and begins to beat the menservants and maidservants, and to eat and drink and get drunk,
the master of that slave will come on a day he does not anticipate and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces{j} and assign him a place with the unfaithful.
And that slave who was aware of what his master wanted yet made no preparation and did not do as he wished will be flogged with many blows.

But the slave who did not know, though he did things worthy of a flogging, will be flogged with few. Much will be demanded from everyone who has been given much, and from the one entrusted with much they will ask still more.
“I came to cast fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!
I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!
Do you imagine I came to give peace on the earth? Not at all, I tell you; rather, division!
For from this time on there will be five in a single house split up, three against two and two against three.

They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.”{k}
He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, at once you say, ‘A rainstorm is coming,’ and so it happens.
And when a south wind is blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens.
Hypocrites! You know how to read the face of earth and sky, but how is it you cannot read this present time?
“Why not decide for yourselves what is just?

As you are going with your opponent to the magistrate, make an effort on the way to settle with him, so that he does not drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison.
I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the very last cent.”{l}

notes.text: Gehenna: the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice (Jer 7:31), used as a name for the place of final punishment.
Two small coins: Greek “two *assaria*.” An assarion was a Roman copper coin worth one sixteenth of a denarius (a day’s wage).
The words in brackets are bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text; they are lacking in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses but present in nearly all other manuscripts.
The verse is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text; it is lacking in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses but present in nearly all other manuscripts.
An hour: or “a cubit”; Greek *pēchys*, a forearm’s length, about 18 inches (45 cm), here probably used figuratively of time.
His kingdom: many manuscripts read “the kingdom of God.”
Keep your belts fastened: literally “Let your loins be girded,” that is, with long robes tucked up for action.
Before midnight or after it: literally “in the second or the third watch.” The Romans divided the night into four watches: about 6–9 p.m., 9 p.m.–midnight, midnight–3 a.m., and 3–6 a.m.
He would not have allowed: many manuscripts read “he would have stayed awake and would not have allowed.”
Cut him in pieces: or “punish him severely.”
Compare Mic 7:6.
Cent: Greek *lepton*, the smallest copper coin, worth about one hundred twenty-eighth of a denarius (a day’s wage).

verses.text: At that very time some people who were there brought him word about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices.
He responded, “Do you imagine that these Galileans, because they underwent such things, were greater sinners than every other Galilean?
By no means, I tell you. But unless you repent, you will every one of you perish as they did.
Or those eighteen on whom the tower at Siloam{a} fell and killed them — do you imagine they were more in debt{b} than all the other people living in Jerusalem?
By no means, I tell you. But unless you repent, you will all perish in the same way.”
He went on to tell this parable: “Someone owned a fig tree that had been planted in his vineyard, and he went to it in search of fruit and found nothing.
So he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look here: for three years I have been coming in search of fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Chop it down! Why should it go on using up the soil?’
But he replied, ‘Sir, leave it alone this year too, until I dig around it and spread manure.
If after this it yields fruit — fine; but if not, you shall cut it down.’”
He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the sabbath.
And there was a woman who for eighteen years had had a spirit that disabled her. She was bent double and quite unable to stand up straight.
When Jesus saw her, he called her over and told her, “Woman, you are set free from your infirmity.”
He laid his hands on her, and at once she was made upright again and began to glorify God.

But the synagogue ruler, angry because Jesus had done a healing on the sabbath, said repeatedly to the people, “Six days there are for working. On those, then, come and get your healing, not on the sabbath day.”
The Lord answered him, “Hypocrites! Does not each of you on the sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it off to water?
And this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan has kept tied up for eighteen long years — was it not right that she be untied from this bond on the sabbath day?”
As he said these things, all his opponents were put to shame, while the whole crowd was delighted at all the glorious things being done by him.
So he said, “What is the kingdom of God like? To what shall I compare it?
It is like a mustard seed that someone took and tossed into his garden. It grew and turned into a tree, and the birds of the sky nested in its branches.”
Once more he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God?
It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in about forty-five pounds of flour,{c} until the whole batch was leavened.”
He journeyed on through towns and villages, teaching and making his way toward Jerusalem.
Someone asked him, “Lord, is it only a few who are being saved?” He said to them,
“Strain every nerve to go in through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to go in and will not manage it.
Once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, you will begin to stand outside knocking and saying, ‘Lord, open up for us!’ But he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’
Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your company, and you taught in our streets.’
And he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Get away from me, all you doers of wrong!’{d}
There will be weeping there and grinding of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets inside God’s kingdom, while you yourselves are being thrown outside.
People will come from east and west, and from north and south, and will recline at table in God’s kingdom.
And note this: there are last ones who will be first, and there are first ones who will be last.”
At that same hour some Pharisees came up and told him, “Leave this place and be on your way, for Herod intends to kill you.”
He replied, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Look, I drive out demons and carry out healings today and tomorrow, and the third day I am brought to completion.’
Yet I must keep going today and tomorrow and the day after that, for it is unthinkable that a prophet should perish anywhere but in Jerusalem.
Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killer of the prophets and stoner of those sent to her! How often I longed to gather your children as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were unwilling!
See, your house is abandoned to you.{e} And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”{f}

notes.text: Siloam: Hebrew *Shiloah*, “sent,” a pool and district in the southeast of Jerusalem (compare John 9:7).
In debt: that is, guilty; sin is often pictured as a debt (compare 11:4).
About forty-five pounds of flour: Greek “three *sata* of wheat flour.” A saton (Hebrew *seah*) was about 13 liters, so the whole was about 10 gallons (39 liters), a very large batch of dough.
Many manuscripts add “desolate.” Compare Jer 12:7; 22:5.
Ps 118:26. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.

verses.text: It happened one sabbath, when he went to eat a meal in the house of one of the leading Pharisees, that they were watching him closely.
And look, before him stood a man suffering from dropsy.{a}
Jesus responded by asking the lawyers and Pharisees, “Is healing on the sabbath permitted, or not?”
But they held their peace. So he took hold of the man, cured him, and let him go.
Then he said to them, “Which of you, if a son{b} or an ox falls into a well, will not haul him up right away on the sabbath day?”
To this they had no reply to make.
Noticing how the guests were picking out the places of honor, he told them a parable:
“Whenever someone invites you to a marriage feast, do not recline in the foremost seat. A guest more eminent than you may have been invited by him,
and the host who invited you both comes and says to you, ‘Make room for this man,’ and then, red-faced, you start to take the lowest place.

Instead, when you are invited, go and recline in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may tell you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all your fellow guests.
For all who exalt themselves will be brought low, and those who humble themselves will be lifted up.”

He also said to his host, “When you put on a midday meal or an evening meal, do not summon your friends, your brothers, your kin, or wealthy neighbors; they might well invite you in return, and you would be paid back.
Rather, when you give a reception, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind.
Then you will be blessed, because they have no means of repaying you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”
On hearing this, one of the dinner guests said to him, “Blessed is whoever will eat bread in God’s kingdom!”
Jesus told him, “A certain man was giving a great dinner and invited many.
At the dinner hour he sent his slave to tell the invited guests, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’
But one and all, they began making excuses. The first told him, ‘I have bought a field, and I am obliged to go out and look at it. Please, consider me excused.’
Another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am on my way to try them out. Please, consider me excused.’
Another said, ‘I have married a wife, and that is why I cannot come.’

On his return the slave told his lord these things. At that the master of the house was enraged and said to his slave, ‘Go out quickly into the broad streets and alleys of the city and bring the poor, the maimed, the blind, and the lame in here.’
Then the slave said, ‘Sir, your order has been carried out, and still there is room.’
So the master told the slave, ‘Go out to the roads and the hedgerows and compel people to come in, so that my house may be filled.
I assure you, none of those men who were invited shall so much as sample my banquet.’”
Large crowds were traveling with him, and he turned and said to them,
“If anyone comes to me and does not hate{c} his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters — yes, and even his own life — he cannot be my disciple.
Whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and reckon up the cost, to see whether he has enough to complete it?
Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is unable to finish, all the onlookers will begin to ridicule him,
saying, ‘This fellow began to build and was not able to finish.’
Or what king, setting out to meet another king in battle, will not sit down first and deliberate whether with ten thousand he is strong enough to face the one coming against him with twenty thousand?
If he cannot, he sends envoys while the other is yet far away and asks what the conditions of peace are.
In the same way, then, none of you who does not say farewell to all his possessions can be my disciple.
“Salt, then, is good; but if even salt loses its taste,{d} with what will its saltiness be restored?
It is of no use for the soil or for the manure heap; people throw it out. Let anyone with ears to hear, hear!”

notes.text: Dropsy: Greek *hydrōpikos*, a disease in which fluid gathers in the tissues, causing swelling.
A son: so the Westcott–Hort text, with P45, P75, Vaticanus, and many others. Some manuscripts read “a donkey” (compare 13:15), and a few “a sheep.”
Hate: a Semitic idiom for loving less or putting in second place (compare Matt 10:37; Gen 29:30–31).
Loses its taste: Greek *mōrainō*, “becomes foolish” or “becomes insipid.” The salt of the region, from the Dead Sea, contained impurities and could lose its savor.

verses.text: Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to listen to him.
And both the Pharisees and the scribes kept grumbling, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.”
So he told them this parable:
“Suppose one of you owns a hundred sheep and loses one of them. Will he not leave the ninety-nine in the open country and go after the lost one until he finds it?
And having found it, he lifts it onto his shoulders, rejoicing,
and on reaching home he calls his friends and neighbors together. ‘Celebrate with me,’ he tells them, ‘for my lost sheep has been found.’
In the same way, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance.
“Or suppose a woman has ten silver coins{a} and loses one. Will she not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search with care until she finds it?
And having found it, she calls her women friends and neighbors together, saying, ‘Celebrate with me, for I have found the coin I lost.’
Just so, I tell you, joy arises before the angels of God over a single sinner who repents.”
He continued: “A certain man had two sons.
The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the portion of the property that falls to me.’ So he divided his livelihood between them.
A few days later the younger son turned everything into cash and went abroad to a distant country, where he squandered his property in reckless living.
When he had spent it all, a severe famine swept that country, and he began to be in want.
So he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to tend pigs.
He longed to fill his stomach{b} with the carob pods{c} the pigs were eating, but no one would give him any.
Coming to himself, he said, ‘My father’s hired workers, all of them, have more bread than they need, while I am perishing here from famine!
I will set off and go to my father, and I will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.
I no longer deserve to be called your son; treat me as one of your hired men.”’
So he got up and came to his own father. But while he was still at a great distance, his father saw him and was moved to pity; running to him, he fell on his neck and kissed him over and over.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I no longer deserve to be called your son. [Treat me as one of your hired men.]’{d}
But the father told his slaves, ‘Quick! Bring out a robe, the finest, and put it on him; put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
Fetch the fattened calf and slaughter it, and let us eat and celebrate;
for this my son was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’ And they began to celebrate.
“Meanwhile his elder son was out in the field. As he came near the house on his way in, he heard music and dancing.
He called one of the servant boys over and inquired what this might mean.
He told him, ‘Your brother has come home, and your father has slaughtered the fattened calf, because he has got him back safe and sound.’
But he grew angry and would not go in. His father came out and kept pleading with him.
He answered his father, ‘Look! All these years I have been slaving for you, and never once disobeyed an order of yours; yet you never gave me so much as a young goat to celebrate with my friends.
But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your livelihood with prostitutes, for him you slaughtered the fattened calf!’
He said to him, ‘My child, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this brother of yours was dead and is alive; he was lost and is found.’”

notes.text: Silver coins: Greek *drachmai*. A drachma was a Greek silver coin worth about a day’s wage for a laborer.
To fill his stomach: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others; many manuscripts read “to fill his belly.”
Carob pods: the pods of the carob tree, used as animal fodder and eaten by the very poor.
The bracketed words are found in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and a few others, but are lacking in P75 and most manuscripts; they may have been added from 15:19.

verses.text: He also told the disciples, “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and charges were brought to him that this man was squandering his property.
So he summoned him and said, ‘What is this I hear about you? Hand in the accounts of your stewardship, for you can no longer act as steward.’
The steward thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my lord is removing me from the stewardship? Digging I have no strength for; begging I would be ashamed of.
I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from the stewardship people will receive me into their homes.’
Then he summoned his master’s debtors one by one. To the first he said, ‘What is the amount you owe my lord?’
He said, ‘Six hundred gallons of olive oil.’{a} He told him, ‘Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write three hundred.’
Then he asked another, ‘And you, how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘Six hundred twenty-five bushels of wheat.’{b} He told him, ‘Take your bill and write five hundred.’
And the master commended the dishonest steward because he had acted shrewdly; for the sons of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.
And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon{c} of unrighteousness, so that when it gives out they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.
“One who is trustworthy in a very little is trustworthy also in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is dishonest also in much.
If, then, you have not proved trustworthy with unrighteous mammon, who will entrust you with what is genuine?
And if you have not been faithful with someone else’s property, who will hand over to you what belongs to you?{d}
No household slave can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to one and scorn the other. You cannot be slaves to God and to mammon.”
The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, were listening to all this, and they sneered at him.
He said to them, “You are the ones who declare yourselves righteous in people’s eyes, but God knows your hearts; for what is lofty among humans is an abomination before God.
“The law and the prophets lasted until John. From then on the good news of God’s kingdom is being proclaimed, and everyone is forcing his way into it.{e}
Yet heaven and earth will sooner pass away than a single stroke{f} of the law fall to the ground.
“Any man who sends his wife away and marries another woman is committing adultery, and anyone who marries a woman sent away by her husband is committing adultery.
“A certain man was rich, and he used to clothe himself in purple and fine linen, enjoying a lavish feast every day.
Before his gateway had been laid a poor man, Lazarus{g} by name, full of ulcers,
who yearned to be fed with the scraps dropping from the rich man’s table.{h} The dogs even came and licked his ulcers.
In time the poor man died and was carried away by the angels to Abraham’s side.{i} The rich man also died and was buried.
And in Hades, where he was in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus at his side.
So he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have pity on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’
But Abraham replied, ‘My child, remember: you in your lifetime got your good things, and Lazarus in the same way got evil things. Now here he is being consoled, while you are in anguish.
Besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor may anyone pass over from there to us.’
Then the rich man said, ‘In that case, father, I ask you to send him to the house of my father —
for I have five brothers — so that he may warn them, lest they too come to this place of torment.’
But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them.’
He said, ‘No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’
He said to him, ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’”

notes.text: Six hundred gallons of olive oil: Greek “a hundred *batoi* of oil.” A batos (Hebrew *bath*) was about 22 liters (6 gallons), so the whole was about 2,200 liters. The reduction is by half.

Six hundred twenty-five bushels of wheat: Greek “a hundred *koroi* of wheat.” A koros (Hebrew *kor*) was about 220 liters (6¼ bushels), so the whole was about 22,000 liters. The reduction is by a fifth.
Mammon: an Aramaic word for wealth or property, here almost personified (also in 16:11, 13).
Your own: some manuscripts read “ours.”
Everyone is forcing his way into it: or “everyone is urged to enter it,” or “everyone is treating it violently”; the meaning of Greek *biazetai* is uncertain here.
Stroke: Greek *keraia*, “little horn,” a small mark distinguishing one letter from another.
Lazarus: a Greek form of *Eleazar*, “God has helped.”
The scraps dropping: literally “the things falling”; many manuscripts read “the crumbs falling.”
Abraham’s side: literally “Abraham’s bosom,” the place of honor beside the host at a banquet (compare John 13:23).

verses.text: He said to his disciples, “Snares that cause people to fall are bound to come, but woe to the one through whom they come!
He would be better off thrown into the sea with a millstone hung around his neck than causing one of these little ones to stumble.
Keep watch over yourselves. If your brother sins, reprove him, and if he repents, forgive him.
Even if seven times in a day he sins against you, and seven times turns back to you and says, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.”
The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!”
The Lord replied, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree,{a} ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.
“Which of you who has a slave plowing or minding sheep will say to him when he comes in from the field, ‘Come along at once and take your place at table’?
Will he not rather tell him, ‘Get my supper ready, put on your apron, and wait on me while I eat and drink; afterward you can eat and drink yourself’?
Does he thank the slave for carrying out his orders?
So it is with you as well. When you have done all you were ordered, say, ‘We are slaves who deserve no credit;{b} we have only done what was our duty.’”
On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between{c} Samaria and Galilee.
As he went into a certain village, ten leprous{d} men met him. They kept their distance
and raised their voices: “Jesus, Master, take pity on us!”
Seeing them, he said, “Go, show yourselves to the priests.”{e} And as they went, they were made clean.
One of them, seeing that he had been healed, turned back, praising God at the top of his voice.
He fell face down at Jesus’ feet, thanking him; and he was a Samaritan.
Jesus responded, “Were not ten made clean? Where are the other nine?
Was no one found to come back and give glory to God except this foreigner?”
And he told him, “Rise and go on your way; your faith has made you well.”{f}
Once, on being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, “The kingdom of God does not come in a way that can be watched for,
nor will people say, ‘See, it is here!’ or ‘There!’ For look, the kingdom of God is within your grasp.”{g}
Then he said to the disciples, “Days are coming when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.
People will say to you, ‘See, there!’ or ‘See, here!’ Do not [go off, or] chase after them.{h}
For just as lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end under heaven to the other, so will the Son of Man be.{i}
Before that, however, he has many things to suffer and must be rejected by this generation.
As things were in Noah’s days, so they will be also in the days of the Son of Man.
People ate, drank, married and were given in marriage, up to the day Noah went into the ark; then the flood came and destroyed every one of them.
It was the same in the days of Lot: they ate, drank, bought, sold, planted, built;
but the day Lot went out from Sodom it rained fire and brimstone out of the sky, and all of them perished.
It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed.
On that day, anyone on the housetop whose goods are in the house must not come down to fetch them; likewise anyone in the field must not turn back for what is behind.
Remember Lot’s wife!{j}
Whoever seeks to keep his life safe will lose it, but whoever loses it will preserve it alive.
I tell you, on that night there will be two in one bed; one will be taken and the other left.
Two women will be grinding grain together; one will be taken and the other left.”
They asked him in reply, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the body is, there the vultures{l} too will gather.”

notes.text: Mulberry tree: Greek *sykaminos*, probably the black mulberry, a tree with deep and extensive roots.
Who deserve no credit: or “unworthy,” “useless”; Greek *achreioi*.
Between: or “through the middle of”; the Greek phrase is unusual, and its precise sense is uncertain.
Leprous: the Greek term for leprosy covered various skin diseases, not only Hansen’s disease.
Compare Lev 14:1–32.
Made you well: or “saved you.”
Within your grasp: or “among you,” “in your midst,” or “within you”; Greek *entos hymōn*.
Do not go off, or chase after them: the bracketed words are bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text; the manuscripts vary in the wording here.
So will the Son of Man be: many manuscripts add “in his day.” The words are lacking in P75, Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and a few others.
Compare Gen 19:26.

Verse 36 is lacking in the Westcott–Hort text and in the earliest manuscripts, including P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus; the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Codex Bezae and some later witnesses add, “Two will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left” (from Matt 24:40).
Vultures: or “eagles”; Greek *aetoi*.

verses.text: He told them a parable about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart.
“In a certain city,” he said, “there was a judge who had no fear of God and no regard for any human being.
In that city there was also a widow who kept coming to him with the plea, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’
For a while he would not. But afterward he said to himself, ‘Granted that I fear neither God nor any person,
still, because this widow keeps pestering me, I will see that she gets justice, or else she will wear me out{a} with her endless coming.’”
And the Lord said, “Listen to what the unjust judge says.
Will not God, then, see justice done for his chosen ones who cry out to him day and night? Will he be slow to help them?{b}
I tell you, he will see justice done for them speedily. Yet when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”
To certain people who were confident in themselves that they were righteous, and who looked down on everyone else, he also told this parable:
“Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
The Pharisee took his stand and prayed thus about himself:{c} ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humankind — swindlers, wrongdoers, adulterers — or even like this tax collector.
Twice a week I fast; a tenth of all I acquire I give.’
But the tax collector, standing far back, would not so much as raise his eyes toward heaven, but kept striking his breast and saying, ‘God, be merciful{d} to me, the sinner!’
I tell you, it was this man, not the other, who went down to his home justified. For everyone who raises himself up will be humbled, while the one who humbles himself will be raised up.”
People were bringing even their babies to him, for him to touch them. When the disciples noticed, they scolded them.
But Jesus summoned them, saying, “Allow the little children to come to me, and stop preventing them; for God’s kingdom belongs to such as these.
Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive God’s kingdom as a little child does will never enter it.”
A certain ruler put this question to him: “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone.
The commandments you know: ‘Do not commit adultery, do not commit murder, do not steal, do not testify falsely, honor your father and your mother.’”{e}
He replied, “I have observed all these from my youth.”
On hearing this, Jesus told him, “There is still one thing you lack. Sell everything you have and distribute it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”
But at these words he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.
Looking at him, Jesus said, “How hard it is for those who possess wealth to make their way into God’s kingdom!
Indeed, it is easier for a camel to pass through a needle’s eye than for a rich person to enter God’s kingdom.”
Those who heard it said, “Then who can be saved?”
He replied, “Things impossible with humans are possible with God.”
Peter said, “Look, we have left what was ours and followed you.”
He told them, “Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of God’s kingdom
who will not receive many times as much in this present time, and in the age to come eternal life.”
Taking the Twelve aside, he said to them, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything written by the prophets about the Son of Man will be accomplished.
He will be delivered up to the nations; they will make sport of him, treat him with contempt, and spit on him;
they will scourge him and put him to death, and on the third day he will rise.”
But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was being said.
When he was approaching Jericho, there was a blind man seated beside the road, begging.
Hearing a crowd going by, he asked what was happening.
They informed him, “Jesus the Nazarene{f} is going past.”
So he shouted, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Those who were in front scolded him to make him be quiet, but he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stopped and ordered the man brought to him. When he had come near, Jesus asked him,
“What do you wish me to do for you?” He answered, “Lord, I want to see again.”
Jesus said to him, “See again! Your faith has made you well.”
Instantly he regained his sight and began following him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

notes.text: Wear me out: Greek *hypōpiazō*, literally “give me a black eye,” perhaps used figuratively.
Will he be slow to help them: or “even though he is patient with them”; the sense of the clause is uncertain.
About himself: or “to himself.” Some manuscripts read “standing by himself, prayed thus.”
Be merciful: Greek *hilasthēti*, “be propitiated,” “be reconciled.”
The Nazarene: Greek *ho Nazōraios*, “the Nazorean,” probably meaning “from Nazareth.”

verses.text: He entered Jericho and was making his way through it.
And there was a man there, Zacchaeus{a} by name, who was a chief tax collector and a wealthy one.
He kept trying to get a look at Jesus, to see who he was, yet he was unable because of the throng, for he was a small man.
So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore-fig tree{b} in order to see him, since Jesus was about to come that way.
When Jesus reached the spot, he looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He came down in haste and gladly welcomed him as his guest.
Everyone who saw it began to grumble, “He has gone in to lodge with a sinful man.”
But Zacchaeus stood his ground and said to the Lord, “Look, half of what I own, Lord, I am giving to the poor; and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I am paying it back four times over.”{c}
Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this household, since he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to look for the lost and to save them.”
As they listened to these things, he added a parable, since he was close to Jerusalem and they imagined that God’s kingdom was to be revealed immediately.
So he said, “A man of noble birth traveled to a far country to obtain royal power for himself and then return.{d}
Summoning ten of his slaves, he handed them ten sums of money, each about a hundred days’ wages,{e} and told them, ‘Put this to work in trade until I come.’
But his citizens hated him, and they sent a delegation after him to say, ‘We will not have this man reign over us.’
When he returned, having received the royal power, he had those slaves to whom he had given the money called to him, to find out what each had gained by trading.
The first came forward and said, ‘Lord, your sum has earned ten sums more.’
He told him, ‘Well done, good slave! Since you proved faithful in a very small matter, take charge of ten cities.’
The second came and said, ‘Your sum, lord, has made five sums.’
He said to him likewise, ‘And you, be over five cities.’
Then the other one came and said, ‘Lord, here is your sum, which I kept stored away in a cloth;
for I feared you, since you are a hard man: you pick up what you never laid down and harvest what you never planted.’
He told him, ‘By your own words I will judge you, you wicked slave! You knew, did you, that I am an exacting man, collecting what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow?
Why then did you not put my money in the bank, so that on my return I could have collected it with interest?’
And to the bystanders he said, ‘Take the sum from him and give it to the one who has the ten.’
They said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten already!’
‘I tell you, to all who have, more shall be given; but from anyone who lacks, even what he does have shall be taken away.
But those enemies of mine, the ones unwilling for me to be king over them, bring them here and execute them in my presence.’”
Having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
When he drew near Bethphage and Bethany,{f} at the hill called the Mount of Olives, he sent off two of the disciples,
saying, “Go into the village opposite. As you enter it you will find a colt tied up that no one has ever yet sat on. Untie it and lead it here.
If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ say this: ‘The Lord needs it.’”
Those who had been sent went off and found things just as he had told them.
As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?”
They answered, “The Lord needs it.”
They brought it to Jesus, threw their cloaks on the colt, and mounted Jesus on it.
As he rode on, people kept spreading their cloaks on the road.
And as he was now approaching the descent from the Mount of Olives, the whole throng of disciples began joyfully to praise God with loud voices for all the mighty works they had seen,
From among the crowd some Pharisees spoke to him: “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”
He answered, “I tell you, if these keep quiet, the stones will shout out.”
As he came near and caught sight of the city, he wept over it,
saying, “If only you had recognized on this day, you of all people, the things that make for peace! But as it is, they are hidden from your eyes.
For days will come upon you when your enemies will throw up a rampart against you, encircle you, and hem you in on every side.
They will dash you to the ground, you and your children within you, and they will not leave one stone on another within you, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.”
Then he went into the temple and began driving out those who were selling,
telling them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’{h} but you have made it a bandits’ cave.”
Day after day he was teaching in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes were seeking to destroy him, and so were the leaders of the people;
yet they could find nothing they could do, for the whole people clung to him as they listened.

notes.text: Zacchaeus: from Hebrew *Zakkai*, “pure” or “innocent.”
Sycamore-fig tree: Greek *sykomorea*, a fig tree with low, spreading branches, not the North American sycamore.
Four times over: compare Exod 22:1; 2 Sam 12:6.
Compare the journey of Archelaus, son of Herod the Great, to Rome in 4 BC to be confirmed as king, and the Jewish delegation that opposed him (Josephus, *Antiquities* 17.299–314).
Ten sums of money, each about a hundred days’ wages: Greek “ten *minas*.” A mina was a sum of a hundred drachmas, each drachma about a day’s wage; so also “sum” in 19:16–25.

Bethphage and Bethany: villages on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives. *Bethphage* means “house of unripe figs”; the meaning of *Bethany* is uncertain, perhaps “house of affliction” or “house of Ananiah.”
Ps 118:26. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.
Isa 56:7; compare Jer 7:11.

verses.text: One day, as he was teaching the people in the temple and proclaiming the good news, the chief priests and the scribes came up together with the elders
and spoke to him: “Tell us by what authority you do these things. Or who is it that gave you this authority?”
In reply he said to them, “I too will put a question to you; tell me:
John’s baptism — was it from heaven, or of human origin?”
They reasoned among themselves, saying, “If we answer, ‘From heaven,’ he will ask, ‘Why did you not believe him?’
But if we answer, ‘Of human origin,’ the whole people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.”
Their answer was that they could not say where it was from.
Jesus told them, “Neither am I telling you by what authority I do these things.”
He began to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard, leased it out to tenant farmers, and went abroad for a long time.
When the season came he dispatched a slave to the farmers, for them to hand over to him some of the fruit of the vineyard; but the farmers beat him and sent him away empty-handed.
He went on to send another slave; that one too they beat and treated shamefully and sent off with nothing.
And he went on to send a third; this one too they wounded and threw out.
Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my son, the beloved one; perhaps they will show him respect.’
But when the tenants saw him, they talked it over with one another: ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so the inheritance may become ours.’
So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What, then, will the owner of the vineyard do to them?
He will come and destroy these tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said, “May it never be!”
Everyone who falls on that stone will be shattered, and anyone on whom it falls, it will crush.”{b}
The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, but they feared the people; for they perceived that he had told this parable against them.
Keeping him under watch, they sent agents posing as honest men, to fasten on some word of his so they could deliver him up to the rule and authority of the governor.
They questioned him: “Teacher, we are aware that what you say and teach is right, and that you do not favor anyone, but truly teach God’s way.
Is it lawful for us to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?”
But he saw through their cunning and said to them,
“Show me a silver coin.{c} Whose image and inscription does it bear?” They said, “Caesar’s.”
He told them, “Then render to Caesar the things that belong to Caesar, and to God the things that belong to God.”
Before the people they could not trap him in his words; amazed at his reply, they said nothing more.
Some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, came to him and questioned him,
saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies, leaving a wife but no child, the man is to take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.{d}
Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died childless;
then the second
and the third took her, and so on; all seven died without leaving children.
Last of all the woman died too.
In the resurrection, then, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.”
Jesus told them, “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage;
but those counted worthy of attaining to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.
Nor can they die anymore, for they are like angels, and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.
And that the dead are raised Moses himself made known, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord ‘the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.’{e}
Now he is not God of the dead but of the living; for to him all are alive.”
Some of the scribes responded, “Teacher, you have spoken well.”
For they no longer dared to question him on anything.
Then he put it to them: “In what sense is the Messiah said to be the son of David?

For David himself says in the book of Psalms,
‘The Lord said to my Lord,
Sit at my right hand

until I set your enemies
as a footstool under your feet.’{f}
David then calls him ‘Lord’; so how is he his son?”
In the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples,
“Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces and the front seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.
They devour widows’ houses, and for show they make long prayers. These will receive the more severe judgment.”

notes.text: Verse 18 echoes Isa 8:14–15 and Dan 2:34–35, 44–45.
A silver coin: literally “a denarius,” a Roman silver coin worth a day’s wage, bearing the emperor’s image and inscription.
Deut 25:5–6; compare Gen 38:8.
Exod 3:6. “The Lord” is Yahweh in the Hebrew of Exod 3:15–16.
Ps 110:1. In the Hebrew, “The Lord said” is “Yahweh said”; “my Lord” is *adoni*, “my master.”

verses.text: Looking up, he saw rich people dropping their gifts into the treasury.
And he noticed a certain needy widow dropping in two tiny copper coins.{a}
And he said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them.
For these all contributed from what they had left over, but she from her want has given her entire livelihood.”
When some were remarking about the temple, how it was adorned with fine stones and votive offerings, he said,
“As for these things you are gazing at, days will come when not one stone here will be left upon another that will not be torn down.”
They asked him, “Teacher, when, then, will these things be, and what will be the sign when they are about to happen?”
He said, “Watch out that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and ‘The time has drawn near.’ Do not go after them.
And when you hear of wars and upheavals, do not be terrified; for these things must take place first, but the end does not follow at once.”
Then he went on to say to them, “Nation will rise up against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.
There will be great earthquakes, and in various places plagues and famines; there will be terrors and great signs from heaven.
But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, handing you over to synagogues and prisons, and you will be led before kings and governors on account of my name.
It will turn out for you as an opportunity for testimony.
So settle it in your hearts not to rehearse your defense beforehand;
for I myself will give you a mouth and wisdom that none of your opponents will be able to withstand or contradict.
You will be betrayed even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death.
You will be hated by all because of my name.
Yet not a hair of your head will perish.
By your endurance you will gain your lives.{b}
“When you see Jerusalem encircled by armies, then know that her desolation has drawn near.
At that time let those who are in Judea run for the hills, let those in the middle of the city leave it, and let those out in the fields not enter it;
for these are days of vengeance, in fulfillment of all that is written.
Alas for women who are pregnant and for those nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress on the land and wrath against this people.
They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all the nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles [are] fulfilled.{c}
“There will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth anguish among nations, bewildered by the roar of the sea and the surging waves.
People will faint from fear and from foreboding of what is coming upon the inhabited world, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.{d}
When these things begin to happen, stand up straight and lift your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”
And he spoke a parable to them: “Consider the fig tree, and every tree.
When they are already budding, you can tell by looking that summer is at hand.
So also you, when you see these things taking place, know that the kingdom of God is near.
Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all things take place.
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
“Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be burdened by dissipation and drunkenness and the cares of daily living, and that day spring upon you unexpectedly
like a snare. For it will come in upon everyone living on the face of all the earth.
But stay awake at every season, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to happen, and to stand before the Son of Man.”
Each day he was teaching in the temple, and each night he would go out and spend the night on the hill called the Mount of Olives.
And all the people would get up early in the morning to come to him in the temple to hear him.{e}

notes.text: Tiny copper coins: Greek *lepta*, the smallest coins in use, each worth about one hundred twenty-eighth of a denarius (a day’s wage).
Gain your lives: Greek *psychē*, “soul” or “life.” Many manuscripts read “you will gain” (future); others read “gain” (imperative).
Are: the Westcott–Hort text brackets the words “and they will be” before “the times of the Gentiles,” and they are lacking in many manuscripts.
Compare Dan 7:13.
After 21:38 a group of manuscripts (family 13) places the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11).

verses.text: The feast of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover, was drawing near.
The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to do away with him, for they were afraid of the people.
Then Satan entered into Judas, the one called Iscariot,{a} who was of the number of the Twelve.
He went off and conferred with the chief priests and officers of the temple guard about how he might betray him to them.
They were delighted and agreed to give him money.
He agreed, and from then on he sought a favorable moment to deliver him up to them apart from the crowd.
The day of Unleavened Bread arrived, the day on which the Passover had to be slaughtered.
Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and get the Passover ready for us to eat.”
They asked him, “Where do you want us to prepare it?”
He told them, “Listen: as you go into the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house he enters,
and say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher asks you, Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’
He will show you a large upstairs room, already furnished. Make the preparations there.”
Off they went, and they found everything as he had said to them; and they made the Passover ready.
When the hour arrived, he took his place at the table, and with him the apostles.
He said to them, “With great longing I have longed to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.
For I tell you that I will never eat it until it finds its fulfillment in God’s kingdom.”
Then he took a cup, gave thanks, and said, “Take this and share it among yourselves.
For I tell you, from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.”
And he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, [[which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you.]]{b}
But see, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me on the table.
For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man through whom he is betrayed!”
And they began to debate among themselves which of them it could be who was about to do this.
A quarrel broke out among them too, over which of them seemed to be the greatest.
But he said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors.
Not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become like the youngest, and the leader like one who serves.
For which is greater: the guest at the table, or the servant? Surely the guest at the table. Yet here among you I am like a servant.
But it is you who have remained with me through my trials.
So I assign to you a kingdom, as my Father assigned one to me,
so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and you will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
“Simon, Simon, look: Satan has asked for you all,{c} so as to sift you as wheat is sifted.
But I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”
Peter said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.”
But Jesus said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have three times denied that you know me.”
He said to them, “When I sent you out without purse or bag or sandals, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.”
He said to them, “But now, whoever has a purse must take it, and likewise a bag; and whoever has no sword must sell his cloak and buy one.
For I say to you that what is written must find its completion in me: ‘And with lawless men he was reckoned.’{d} For what concerns me is coming to its end.”
They said, “Lord, look, here are two swords.” He said to them, “It is enough.”
He went out and made his way, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives; and the disciples followed him.
When he reached the place, he said to them, “Pray that you may not come into testing.”{e}
Then he withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, knelt down, and prayed,
“Father, if it is your will, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, let your will be done, not mine.”
[[Then an angel from heaven appeared to him and strengthened him.
And being in anguish, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground.]]{f}
When he rose from prayer and came to the disciples, he found them sleeping for grief.
“Why are you asleep?” he asked them. “Rise and pray, so that you do not enter into testing.”
While he was still speaking, a crowd appeared, and the man called Judas, one of the Twelve, was leading them. He came near to Jesus to kiss him.
But Jesus asked him, “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?”
When those around him saw what was coming, they said, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?”
And one of them struck the high priest’s slave and cut off his right ear.
But Jesus answered, “Stop! No more of this!” And he touched the ear and healed him.
Then Jesus said to those who had come out against him — chief priests, officers of the temple guard, and elders — “Have you come out with swords and clubs as if against a bandit?
When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not stretch out your hands against me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.”
They seized him, led him away, and brought him into the high priest’s house. Peter was following at a distance.
When they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat among them.
A servant girl, seeing him seated in the firelight, stared at him and said, “This man also was with him.”
But he disowned him: “Woman, I don’t know him.”
A little later someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not.”
About an hour later another kept insisting, “Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.”
But Peter answered, “Man, what you are saying I do not know.” And immediately, before he had finished speaking, a rooster crowed.
The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said to him, “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.”
[And he went outside and wept bitterly.]{g}
The men who were holding Jesus began mocking him as they beat him.
They covered his face and questioned him: “Prophesy! Who was it that hit you?”
And they said many other insulting things against him.
At daybreak the elders of the people met together, chief priests as well as scribes, and they brought him before their Sanhedrin,{h} saying,
“If you are the Messiah, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you will not believe,
and if I ask you, you will not answer.
But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.”{i}
All of them said, “Are you, then, the Son of God?” He said to them, “You say that I am.”
Then they said, “What further need of testimony do we have? We ourselves have heard it from his own lips.”

notes.text: Iscariot: perhaps “man of Kerioth” (a town in Judea); the meaning is uncertain.

Which is given for you … poured out for you: the Westcott–Hort text places these words in double brackets as one of the “Western non-interpolations,” since they are absent from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses (some of which also reorder 22:17–19a). They are present in P75 (as reported in the critical editions), Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and nearly all other manuscripts, and modern critical editions (NA, SBLGNT) print them as part of the text.
You all: the Greek pronoun is plural; in 22:32 “you” is singular, addressed to Simon.
Testing: or “temptation”; so also in 22:46.

The angel and the sweat like drops of blood (22:43–44) are placed in double brackets in the Westcott–Hort text. The verses are lacking in early and important witnesses, including P75 (as reported), Vaticanus, the first corrector of Sinaiticus, and others, and some manuscripts mark them as doubtful; but they are present in the original hand of Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, and many others, and were known to second-century writers. A few manuscripts (family 13) place them after Matt 26:39.
The Westcott–Hort text places 22:62 in single brackets, since it is lacking in some Old Latin witnesses; it is present in almost all Greek manuscripts.
Sanhedrin: the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest.
Compare Ps 110:1; Dan 7:13.

verses.text: Then the whole assembly of them rose and brought him before Pilate.
They began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding the payment of taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be Messiah, a king.”
Pilate questioned him: “Are you the King of the Jews?” In answer he said to him, “You say so.”
Pilate then declared to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no grounds for a charge against this man.”
But they pressed all the harder, saying, “He stirs up the people with his teaching throughout all Judea; he began in Galilee and has come even here.”
On hearing this, Pilate inquired whether the man was a Galilean.
Learning that he belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction, he referred him to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem during those days.
Herod was overjoyed to see Jesus, for he had been wanting to see him for a long while, because of what he had heard about him, and he was hoping to watch some sign performed by him.
He questioned him at length, but Jesus made him no reply.
Meanwhile the chief priests and the scribes stood there, vehemently accusing him.
Herod and his soldiers treated him with contempt and made a mockery of him; then, dressing him in a splendid robe, he sent him back to Pilate.
That very day Herod and Pilate became friends with each other, for before this they had been at enmity.
Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers, and the people,
and said to them, “You brought me this man as one who leads the people astray. Now look: I examined him in your presence and found in him no basis for the charges you bring against him.
Nor did Herod, since he has returned him to us. See, nothing worthy of death has been done by him.
So I will have him flogged and let him go.”
But they all shouted out together, “Away with this man! Release Barabbas{b} to us!”
He was someone who had been thrown into prison for an uprising that had taken place in the city, and for murder.
Pilate addressed them once more, wishing to release Jesus,
but they kept shouting back, “Crucify, crucify him!”
A third time he spoke to them: “Why? What wrong has this man done? I have found in him no cause deserving death. So I will have him flogged and release him.”
But they kept pressing him with loud cries, demanding that he be crucified, and their voices prevailed.
Pilate gave sentence that what they asked should be done.
He set free the one whom they requested, who had been put in prison for rebellion and murder; but Jesus he delivered up to their will.
As they led him away, they seized a certain Simon of Cyrene,{c} who was coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry behind Jesus.
A large number of the people followed him, among them women who were beating their breasts and wailing for him.
But Jesus turned toward them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, stop weeping over me. Weep over yourselves instead, and over your children.
For look, days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed.’
At that time they will start saying to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us!’ and to the hills, ‘Hide us!’{d}
For if they treat the green tree like this, what will become of the dry?”
Two others also, who were criminals, were being led away with him to be executed.
When they came to the place called the Skull,{e} they crucified him there, and the criminals too, one on his right and one on his left.
[[And Jesus was saying, “Father, forgive them, since they do not understand what they are doing.”]]{f} Then they cast lots to share out his garments.{g}
The people stood by, watching; and the rulers too were sneering, saying, “Others he saved; let him save himself, if this is God’s Messiah, the Chosen One!”
The soldiers joined in the mockery, approaching him and holding out sour wine to him,
and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!”
Above him there was also a placard: “This is the King of the Jews.”
One of the criminals hanging there kept insulting him: “Are you not the Messiah? Save yourself, and us!”
But the other rebuked him, saying, “Have you no fear of God, since you are under the same sentence?
And for us it is just, since we are receiving what is due for what we did; but this one has done nothing improper.”
Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into{h} your kingdom.”
Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.”
By now it was about noon, and darkness fell over all the land{i} until three in the afternoon,{j}
the sun’s light having failed;{k} and the curtain of the temple was torn down the middle.
Then Jesus, crying out with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.”{l} Having said this, he breathed his last.
The centurion, seeing what took place, gave glory to God and said, “Surely this was a righteous man.”
And the crowds that had come together to view this sight, once they had seen the things that happened, returned home striking their breasts.
But all who knew him, and the women who had accompanied him from Galilee, stood far off and saw these things.
Now there was a man named Joseph, a member of the council, a good and righteous man,
who had not consented to their decision and action. He came from Arimathea, a Jewish town, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God.
This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
He took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb cut in the rock, where no one had ever yet been laid.
It was the day of Preparation, and the sabbath was beginning to dawn.{m}
The women who had come with him from Galilee followed after, and they saw the tomb and how his body was laid.
Then they went back and prepared spices and ointments. And on the sabbath they rested according to the commandment.{n}

notes.text: Verse 17 is lacking in the Westcott–Hort text and in the earliest manuscripts, including P75, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus; the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Many later manuscripts add, “For he had to release one man to them at the festival” (compare Matt 27:15; Mark 15:6), some of them after 23:19.
Barabbas: Aramaic, “son of the father” or “son of Abba.”
Cyrene: a city in North Africa (in modern Libya) with a large Jewish community.
The Skull: Latin *Calvaria*, from which comes “Calvary”; in Aramaic, *Golgotha*.

The prayer “Father, forgive them…” is placed in double brackets in the Westcott–Hort text. It is lacking in early and diverse witnesses, including P75 (as reported), Vaticanus, the first hand of Codex Bezae, and some early versions; it is present in Sinaiticus (original and later hands), Alexandrinus, and most manuscripts. NA and SBLGNT print it within double brackets.
Into: Greek *eis*. Many manuscripts read “in” (*en*) your kingdom, that is, “in your royal power.”
Land: or “earth.”
About noon … three in the afternoon: literally “about the sixth hour … until the ninth hour,” counted from sunrise.

The sun’s light having failed: Greek *tou hēliou ekleipontos*, the reading of the Westcott–Hort text (with P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus); the verb can be used of an eclipse. Many manuscripts read “and the sun was darkened.”
Beginning to dawn: Greek *epiphōskō*, used here of the start of the sabbath at sunset on Friday.
Exod 20:10; Deut 5:14.

verses.text: On the first day of the week, at early dawn, they came to the tomb bringing the spices they had prepared.
They found the stone rolled away from the tomb,
yet on going inside they found no body [[of the Lord Jesus]].{a}
And as they stood perplexed over this, look, two men stood by them in clothing that flashed like lightning.
Filled with fear, the women bent their faces toward the earth; and the men asked them, “Why do you seek the living one among the dead?
[[He is not here, but has been raised.]]{b} Recall how he spoke to you while he was still in Galilee,
saying that the Son of Man must be handed over into the hands of sinful people, be crucified, and on the third day rise again.”
Then they remembered his words,
and returning [from the tomb]{c} they reported all these things to the Eleven and to all the rest.
It was Mary Magdalene,{d} Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles.
But these words seemed to them like nonsense, and they would not believe the women.
[[But Peter got up and ran to the tomb; stooping to look in, he saw the linen wrappings lying by themselves; and he went home, wondering at what had happened.]]{e}
And look, on that very day two of them were traveling to a village about seven miles{f} away from Jerusalem, whose name was Emmaus,
and they were conversing with each other about all these events.
As they talked and debated, Jesus himself drew near and began walking along with them,
but their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
He said to them, “What are these words you are exchanging with one another as you walk?” And they stood still, their faces downcast.
One of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know what has happened there in these days?”
He asked them, “What things?” They told him, “The things about Jesus the Nazarene, who was a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people;
how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to be condemned to death and crucified him.
But we had been hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel. And besides all this, it is now the third day since these things took place.
Moreover, some women from our group astounded us. They went to the tomb early in the morning,
and when they did not find his body, they came back saying they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he is alive.
Some of those with us went off to the tomb and found it just as the women had said; but him they did not see.”
Then he said to them, “How foolish you are, and how slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!
Was it not necessary for the Messiah to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?”
And beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them the things concerning himself in all the Scriptures.
They came near the village to which they were going, and he acted as though he were going farther.
But they urged him strongly, saying, “Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now nearly over.” So he went in to stay with them.
When he had reclined at table with them, he took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and began handing it to them.
Then their eyes were opened, and they recognized him; and he vanished from their sight.
And they said to one another, “Did not our hearts burn inside us as he spoke to us along the way, as he laid open the Scriptures for us?”
They got up that same hour and returned to Jerusalem, and they found the Eleven and those with them gathered together,
who were saying, “The Lord has really been raised, and he has appeared to Simon!”
They in turn related the things on the road, and how they had come to know him in the breaking of the bread.
While they were still talking about these things, he himself stood among them [[and said to them, “Peace to you.”]]{g}
But they were alarmed and frightened, supposing that what they saw was a spirit.
He said to them, “Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts?
Look at my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.”
[[And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.]]{h}
While in their joy they still could not believe it and were marveling, he said to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?”
They gave him a piece of broiled fish,{i}
and taking it he ate it as they watched.
Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.”
Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures,
and he said to them, “Thus it is written, that the Messiah is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day,
and that repentance for{j} the forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all the nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
You are witnesses of these things.
And look, I am sending forth the promise of my Father on you; you, however, are to remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.”
Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them.
While he was blessing them, he parted from them [[and was carried up into heaven]].{k}
And they [[worshiped him and]]{l} returned to Jerusalem with great joy,
and they were continually in the temple, blessing God.{m}

notes.text: Of the Lord Jesus: these words are placed in double brackets in the Westcott–Hort text as one of the “Western non-interpolations” in Luke 24 (see also 24:6, 12, 36, 40, 51, 52). They are absent only from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses, but present in P75 (as reported), Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and nearly all other manuscripts; NA and SBLGNT print them. Some manuscripts read “of Jesus.”

He is not here, but has been raised: a “Western non-interpolation” (see 24:3); lacking in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses, but present in P75 (as reported), Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and almost all others. The verb may also be rendered “he has risen.”
From the tomb: the Westcott–Hort text brackets these words, which are lacking in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin and Armenian witnesses.
Magdalene: “of Magdala,” a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee; the name may mean “tower.”

The whole of 24:12 is a “Western non-interpolation” in the Westcott–Hort text (see 24:3); it is lacking in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses, but present in P75 (as reported), Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and nearly all others, and is printed by NA and SBLGNT. Compare John 20:3–10.
About seven miles: Greek “sixty stadia,” about 11 kilometers. Some manuscripts, including Sinaiticus, read “one hundred sixty stadia” (about 18 miles; 30 kilometers).

The words “and said to them, ‘Peace to you’” are a “Western non-interpolation” in the Westcott–Hort text (see 24:3); lacking in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses, but present in P75 (as reported) and nearly all others. Some manuscripts add, “It is I; do not be afraid” (compare John 6:20).

The whole of 24:40 is a “Western non-interpolation” in the Westcott–Hort text (see 24:3); lacking in Codex Bezae, some Old Latin witnesses, and the Old Syriac, but present in P75 (as reported) and nearly all others. Compare John 20:20.
Broiled fish: many later manuscripts add “and some honeycomb.”
For: Greek *eis*, the reading of the Westcott–Hort text (with P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus); many manuscripts read “and” (*kai*), “repentance and forgiveness of sins.”

And was carried up into heaven: a “Western non-interpolation” in the Westcott–Hort text (see 24:3); lacking in the original hand of Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, and some Old Latin and Syriac witnesses, but present in P75 (as reported), Vaticanus, and most others.

Worshiped him and: a “Western non-interpolation” in the Westcott–Hort text (see 24:3); lacking in Codex Bezae, some Old Latin witnesses, and the Old Syriac, but present in P75 (as reported), Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and most others.
Blessing God: many manuscripts read “praising and blessing God”; Codex Bezae reads “praising God.” Many later manuscripts add “Amen.”
